title: Given an array and a target value, count how many triplets have a sum strictly less than the target. (GeeksforGeeks: Count triplets with sum smaller than X)
shortTitle: Triplets with Smaller Sum (Two Pointers with Counting)
keyPoints: When the fixed + left + right sum is below the target, every pair from left+1 to right also qualifies
Add the entire span (right - left) to the count in one step, not one by one
This batch counting is what makes the algorithm O(n^2) instead of O(n^3)
If the sum is at or above the target, shrink from the right to try a smaller sum
Only a count is needed, so no deduplication or storage of triplets is required
To list the actual triplets, enumerate the span explicitly, trading time for the full listing

s1_definition.oneliner: When left plus right is under target, every pair between them also qualifies, so add the whole span, not just one.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Triplets with Smaller Sum** – count the number of triplets whose sum is strictly less than a given target.
- **Sort + fix + sweep** – same structure as 3Sum: sort the array, fix each element, two-pointer sweep the rest.
- **Batch counting** – when the fixed element plus left and right values is below the target, every element between left and right also forms a valid triplet, so add the span (right - left) to the count at once.
- **Complexity** – O(n^2) time from the outer loop times the linear sweep; O(1) extra space.
- **Count only** – no deduplication or storage is needed because only the count is required.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh at the National Bank of India wants to know how many ways he can pick three fee amounts whose total stays strictly under a regulatory cap. He sorts the fees, fixes one, and uses Priya's two-pointer sweep. The clever part: when the fixed fee plus the smallest and largest of the remaining pair is already under the cap, pairing that smallest with every fee up to the largest is also under the cap, so he counts the entire block in one shot.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting triplets whose sum is strictly less than a target uses the familiar sort-fix-sweep structure with one crucial addition: batch counting. When the fixed element plus the left and right values is already below the target, every element between left and right also forms a valid triplet with the fixed element and the left value. Adding the entire span (right - left) to the count in one step is what makes the algorithm O(n^2) instead of O(n^3).

Because only a count is needed and not the triplets themselves, there is no deduplication or storage, keeping memory constant. If the requirement changed to listing the actual triplets, you would enumerate the span explicitly, consciously trading time for the full listing.

In a compliance rule at the National Bank of India, the bank charges several kinds of fees, and a regulation requires that any bundle of exactly three fees applied together must total strictly less than a cap. The compliance team needs the count of safe three-fee bundles across a long fee schedule to report the proportion that complies. The span-counting two-pointer approach gives the exact count quickly.

The senior-level point is that the batch count is the heart of this problem. A naive adaptation that increments the count by one per triplet would be cubic and miss the batching entirely. Interviewers test whether you see that when the sum is below the threshold, the entire span qualifies.

Remember one sentence: when the sum is under the target, every pair between left and right also qualifies, so add the whole span in one shot.
